item.title: Anthropic makes historic Nasdaq debut amid AI industry promise and risks, marking a key Wall Street test in 2026
item.description: Anthropic, an AI company, has made its debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange, highlighting both the potential and challenges of artificial intelligence in the financial markets. This event represents a significant milestone for AI firms seeking public investment and scrutiny. The company's listing comes at a time when AI technologies are under intense evaluation for their impact on industries and society. Anthropic's public offering will serve as a barometer for investor confidence in AI's future, balancing optimism about innovation with concerns over risks and regulation.

item.title: Anthropic's Claude AI solves two longstanding open problems in black hole physics related to quantum gravity and phase transitions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic's AI system Claude has completed two significant calculations in theoretical physics concerning black holes and quantum gravity. It resolved a 20-year-old problem by showing that a sudden phase transition associated with black hole formation persists even when spacetime loses a definite shape, confirming that this phenomenon is inherent to the underlying quantum theory. Claude also determined the exact limit of a bootstrapping technique used to test candidate quantum gravity theories in a simplified two-dimensional universe model. The first problem involved completing a complex calculation originally proposed in 2003, which had remained unsolved due to the breakdown of classical spacetime concepts at small scales. Claude achieved this by running multiple instances of itself to independently verify parts of the calculation. The second problem addressed the challenge of setting a precise upper bound on the mass of the lightest black hole in a two-dimensional theoretical universe, refining previous numerical approximations and narrowing the search for consistent quantum gravity theories. These breakthroughs provide new insights into the nature of black holes and quantum gravity, demonstrating that certain features of black hole formation are robust across different theoretical frameworks. The results also advance methods for testing and constraining quantum gravity theories, potentially guiding future research in fundamental physics.

item.title: Jacob Coxon and Robin Hanson debate whether governments should slow development of frontier AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Jacob Coxon and Robin Hanson engage in a video debate discussing the potential need for government intervention to slow the advancement of frontier artificial intelligence. The conversation explores differing perspectives on the risks and benefits associated with rapid AI development.

item.title: Researchers analyze why sub-4-bit quantization causes accuracy collapse in Vision CNNs and evaluate mixed-precision recovery limits on ImageNet and ARM/x86 CPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers systematically studied the causes of accuracy collapse in Vision CNNs compressed below 4-bit precision, focusing on ResNet and EfficientNet models evaluated on the ImageNet-1k validation set. They found that degradation is nonlinear and concentrated in late-stage layers, and that selectively retaining less than 5% of activations in 8-bit precision can recover up to 92% of lost accuracy during aggressive compression. The study also assessed deployment performance on ARM and x86 CPUs, revealing that while low-bit quantization reduces memory usage, software bit-unpacking can slow execution by 1.48x to 21.5x depending on batch size, highlighting a trade-off between model size and edge throughput. These findings offer practical guidance for deploying sub-4-bit quantized vision models without severely impacting hardware performance.

item.title: Researchers apply self-rewarded reinforcement learning to improve structure and length of medical explanations in small language models using Mistral-7B and PPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated whether a lightweight reinforcement learning step could enhance the structure of medical explanations generated by small language models (SLMs) without relying on human preference labels. Using the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B model, they applied Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation on 2,000 medical prompts derived from Meerkat, guided by a self-supervised reward favoring longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU resulted in a stable increase in average reward. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations showed that the RL-tuned model produced longer, more organized, multi-point medical explanations while preserving the underlying content. The study discusses both the potential and limitations of using self-rewarded reinforcement learning to shape the style of medical explanations in small language models.

item.title: Researchers evaluate global self-attention and weight sharing in EfficientNet-B0 vision backbones, finding attention adapters improve ImageNet accuracy and alternating shared blocks reduce parameters with minimal loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated the impact of global self-attention and recurrent weight sharing in compact convolutional backbones using EfficientNet-B0 on ImageNet-1k. They found that inserting lightweight self-attention adapters at multiple stages improved accuracy beyond a plain MBConv trunk, while multi-scale feature pyramids alone did not. Additionally, alternating two shared block templates in repeated MBConv blocks reduced model parameters by 10.9% and recovered most accuracy compared to unshared controls. The study showed that learned attention amplitude increased with semantic depth, and that naive kernel averaging severely degraded accuracy. The alternating shared block approach added minimal parameters for pass-specific BatchNorm statistics and regained accuracy quickly during training. These findings clarify where global context and weight sharing can be effectively applied in compact vision models to balance efficiency and performance.

item.title: Researchers introduce Rational Sparse Autoencoder with trainable rational function replacing fixed encoder activations, improving reconstruction fidelity at matched sparsity across language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces fixed encoder nonlinearities like ReLU with a trainable rational function to improve the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off in sparse autoencoders. The RSAE is designed with a two-stage pipeline involving initialization from pre-trained weights and fine-tuning under a sparsity-regularized objective, maintaining the same sparsity level as the baseline models. Testing on residual-stream activations from three open-weight language models and across various baseline activation families, the RSAE consistently improves reconstruction fidelity without increasing sparsity. The upgrade adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and requires between 4 and 25 minutes of training on a single consumer GPU, demonstrating practical efficiency alongside theoretical advantages.

item.title: Researchers present AMP1, a generalist AI model that controls robot manipulators with state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across multiple benchmarks and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce agentic manipulation policies (AMPs) and present AMP1, a generalist AI model that directly commands robot manipulators without task-specific training or demonstrations. AMP1 achieves an 85.6% zero-shot success rate on the RoboLab-120 benchmark, outperforming specialist vision-language-action and world-action models, and succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robot types. The model develops its own manipulation strategies and, with added persistent memory, can learn from experience to further reduce failure rates on bimanual tasks. AMP1 operates unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation settings, demonstrating greater generality and robustness than specialist policies. The research suggests that AMPs provide a promising foundation for future robot manipulation, with code and videos available for further exploration.

item.title: Researchers introduce LLM Complexity metric to quantify problem difficulty in large language model inference, revealing divergence from classical time complexity and enabling improved fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose LLM Complexity, a new metric that measures problem difficulty for large language models (LLMs) by analyzing the accuracy-token curve, challenging the assumption that token usage aligns with classical time complexity. They find that diverse LLMs produce consistent task difficulty rankings under this metric, which they use to develop an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning that enhances accuracy while reducing token consumption. The study also shows that LLM Complexity generalizes well to real-world tasks, correlating more stably across models than human-annotated difficulty labels.

item.title: Researchers analyze what knowledge reinforcement learning inherits from LLM judges in 814 runs teaching 7-8B models to answer or abstain on closed-book questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted 814 reinforcement learning runs to study how large language model (LLM) judges influence 7-8 billion parameter models trained to answer closed-book questions or abstain. They found that specific knowledge about single answers does not transfer; models memorize rewarded wrong answers only for those questions. However, judges' general beliefs about question types affect model behavior, such as increased refusal rates on certain categories, which standard accuracy metrics do not reveal. The study showed that a judge rejecting most correct answers about capitals of former states caused models to refuse nearly all such questions, though the knowledge was not forgotten and models could answer correctly when abstention was blocked. Rewarding models based on consensus among their own untrained samples, without external labels or judges, achieved similar results to using an answer key, suggesting judges do not need intrinsic knowledge to guide training effectively.

item.title: Researchers evaluate transfer effectiveness of post-hoc demographic framing mitigation policies on gender and age contrasts in climate messages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied post-hoc rewriting methods to reduce demographic disparities in large language model-generated text when the original model is inaccessible. They analyzed 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts in demographic-conditioned climate messages, comparing fixed and adaptive editing policies using independent evaluators to assess framing disparity. The study found that a fixed policy targeting messages with lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transferred inconsistently, while an adaptive policy proposing edits on both sides but accepting at most one improved disparity reduction in most comparisons, though with higher preservation risk. Policies editing both messages achieved larger disparity reductions on fewer pairs. The results suggest that mitigation effectiveness varies across objectives, evaluators, prompts, and editing strategies, highlighting the need to report transfer outcomes comprehensively.

item.title: Researchers evaluate confidence methods for zero-shot classification in 11 open-weight LLMs, finding logit-based scoring improves discrimination over black-box methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers compared black-box and white-box confidence estimation methods for zero-shot text classification using 11 open-weight large language models (1B-32B parameters) across five datasets with 3 to 151 labels. They found that while confidence method choice rarely affected accuracy, logit-based scoring methods significantly improved discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) compared to black-box approaches (AUROC 0.57-0.66). The study also introduced decision-only scoring, which reduces decoding steps by 88-96% on large label sets with comparable performance to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method combinations, including Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B, performed competitively with a commercial classifier.

item.title: Researchers investigate continuous location representations to improve spatial generalization in large language models, evaluating on geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers distinguish geospatial memory from spatial generalization in large language models (LLMs), focusing on whether continuous location representations enhance the ability to predict geographic descriptions for unobserved locations. They introduce a latent spatial field concept, projecting continuous spatial encodings into the model's embedding space as spatial tokens, and evaluate this approach using new geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London. The study assesses geospatial captioning to test both memory and generalization, alongside a geospatial grounding model to evaluate the usefulness of generated location-description pairs for mapping text to geographic space. Results across multiple LLM families show that continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations compared to textual coordinates and provide modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Additional analysis supports the presence of spatially organized geographic representations within the models.

item.title: Researchers introduce CaRR framework to improve diffusion language model quality under low inference budgets using commitment-aware refinement and recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present CaRR, a training-free framework designed to enhance the output quality of diffusion language models at low inference budgets by employing updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within existing edit schedules. CaRR includes Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) and Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) modules that operate without additional backbone forwards to refine and recover candidate outputs. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that CaRR consistently improves average accuracy over native editable diffusion language models, with the largest gains observed under tight inference budgets, including a 7.44 percentage point increase at one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget.

item.title: Review examines clinical large language models' reasoning errors and proposes neuro-symbolic methods to verify logic and improve AI safety in medical applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: This review analyzes how clinical large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible but invalid reasoning that static benchmarks fail to detect, leading to hallucinations and flawed inferences. It covers four paradigms: the origins of clinical hallucination, the agentic hallucination cascade in multi-agent systems, process reward modeling for step-level supervision, and neuro-symbolic grounding that uses formal logic and knowledge graphs to constrain neural outputs. The authors argue that current evaluation and regulation focus on final answer accuracy without verifying reasoning steps, which poses safety risks in clinical AI. The paper highlights that systems incorporating symbolic veto layers within their encoded domains can provide verifiable guarantees and improve safety metrics, though existing studies are limited to simulations or small samples and are not directly comparable to neural baselines. It proposes a conceptual framework linking agentic failure modes to symbolic intervention points and emphasizes that clinical AI safety depends heavily on system architecture. The authors advocate for certification processes that audit reasoning trajectories alongside static benchmark accuracy to ensure responsible deployment of medical AI.

item.title: Researchers propose PoolDPP, a determinantal point process-based method to improve diversity in language model sampling with theoretical guarantees and empirical gains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce PoolDPP, a method that models diverse generation from language models as sampling subsets from a determinantal point process (DPP), balancing item quality and diversity by repelling similar outputs. Since exact inference is intractable, PoolDPP draws a candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weights candidates, and applies a $K$-DPP sampler or a greedy MAP variant for deterministic selection, with a proven finite-sample bound on approximation quality. Empirical results show PoolDPP extends the quality-diversity frontier in open-ended text generation and improves precision-recall trade-offs in ambiguous text-to-SQL tasks and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, increasing diversity without sacrificing accuracy at comparable sample sizes.

item.title: Researchers introduce InflEns, a game-theoretic mixture of LoRA experts for data allocation that predicts expert specialization and routing without training explicit gates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present InflEns, a framework that uses a location game in a fixed prompt-trait space to allocate training data and inference routing among LoRA experts, enabling prediction of which expert will perform best on a given prompt. Evaluated on seven safety-related benchmarks, InflEns shows that the expert with the highest share of prompts achieves the lowest negative log-likelihood on about 90% of cases, outperforming random allocations and matching learned gating methods without explicit gate training. The fixed routing allows identification and retraining of harmful experts, significantly reducing attack success while maintaining instruction following. InflEns offers control over expert specialization through kernel choice, trait-space geometry, and expert count, and can be extended to various encoders and data distributions.

item.title: Researchers introduce PosteriorBench to evaluate algorithms for efficient behavior posterior sampling in language models using 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present PosteriorBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate algorithms that sample from a language model's distribution over transcripts exhibiting rare behaviors. The benchmark includes 21 tasks on the Qwen3.5-0.8B model with behavior probabilities ranging from 10^-5 to 10^-1, using exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses to measure compute cost and sample fidelity via KL divergence. The study finds that existing methods either lack efficiency or faithfulness: simple prompting methods are computationally cheap but yield high divergence from the true posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often too costly, and prior training methods do not improve performance. The researchers highlight that developing a cost-effective posterior sampler remains an open challenge and provide code and data to facilitate progress in this area.

item.title: Researchers propose a deterministic reconciliation contract for large language model decisions using cross-prompt and cross-model checks to improve auditability and error detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a reconciliation contract for large language models (LLMs) that commits to a target model's greedy answer (the anchor) and verifies it with one or two checks from alternate prompts or different model families. This method returns one of five outcomes, acting only on agreement, to ensure decisions are auditable and reproducible despite generation variability on hosted APIs. The approach was evaluated on 48,000 model-item pairs across 6,000 questions, showing that pooling samples from different model families improves semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points compared to same-model temperature checks, which performed weakest. The contract automates decisions on 70% of items while still acting on 16% of errors, outperforming pooled entropy detectors with fewer samples under various tie-breaker conventions. It provides a fixed committed answer, explicit outcomes, and replayable decision records, addressing reproducibility challenges in LLM pipelines that make discrete decisions unattended.

item.title: Researchers propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation to adapt inference schedules for diffusion language models, certifying cost reductions across tasks and models with error guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a method that adapts denoising schedules in diffusion language models based on task, model, and sampler characteristics to reduce computational cost while preserving output quality. TCDA uses calibration data and statistical bounds to certify the cheapest feasible inference schedule or revert to the full schedule, maintaining an asymptotic error probability below a set threshold. The approach was tested on seven datasets and two model families, achieving denoiser evaluation reductions ranging from 1.33 to 8 times depending on the task and model. Validation on fresh data confirmed the reliability of schedule selections, with false certification rates below 2%. The study also found that schedule effectiveness varies with task and model scale, and that reproducible comparisons require fixing the random time grid used by the ELF reference sampler.

item.title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.

item.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.26248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

item.title: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.29486v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

item.title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.04236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

item.title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.38169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding steps; spatially, errors in different key rows affect model outputs differently, while state magnitudes vary substantially along both rows and columns. Motivated by these observations, we propose STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization framework for Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates precision according to error magnitude and memory lifetime, and jointly fits key-row and value-column scales based on state distributions and key-row impact on output error. Experiments on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct across both long- and short-generation benchmarks show that STEPQuant closely matches FP32-state accuracy under a nominal 6-bit budget and outperforms uniform INT8 in its 4-bit configuration. Integrated into SGLang with optimized GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant achieves over 5x recurrent-state compression and reduces total serving memory by up to 68.7%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant.

item.title: Capturing In-Context Learning Dynamics with Task Operators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.01054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to perform new tasks from demonstrations without weight updates. However, every ICL inference requires processing the full set of examples, resulting in inefficient deployments, and how ICL works mechanistically is not fully understood. Prior work compresses ICL into fixed activation vectors extracted from specific layers or positions, but these input-independent interventions fail on complex tasks where the output depends on fine-grained interactions with the input. By analyzing the ICL forward pass, we show that each attention head's output is an affine transformation of its context-masked counterpart, and that the parameters of this transformation are empirically stable across samples for a given task. Building on this, we introduce Task Operator (TO), which replays this transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection. Across lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning tasks, TO achieves the best overall performance among prior methods and substantially narrows the gap between zero-shot inference and ICL. We further show that the extracted knowledge concentrates in a task-specific sparse circuit across layers and positions, and that averaging operators from disjoint demonstration batches enables effective many-shot scaling without expanding the context window. Our code is available at https://github.com/gzxiong/task_operator.

item.title: AVSD: Adaptive-View Self-Distillation by Balancing Consensus and Teacher-Specific Privileged Signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.20643v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-distillation enables language models to learn on-policy from their own trajectories by using the same model as both student and teacher, with the teacher being conditioned on privileged information unavailable to the student. Such information can come in different types or views, such as solutions, demonstrations, feedback, or final answers. This setup provides dense token-level feedback without relying on a separate external model, but creates a fundamental asymmetry: the teacher may rely on view-specific information that the student cannot access at inference time. Moreover, the best type of privileged information is often task-dependent, making it difficult to choose a single teacher view. In this work, we address both these challenges jointly by introducing AVSD (Adaptive-View Self-Distillation), a novel method of self-distillation with multiple privileged-information views, which reconstructs token-level supervision by separating stable cross-view consensus from view-specific residual signals. AVSD identifies the consensus signal shared across views, which provides a reliable update direction, and then selectively adds the view-specific residual signal to adjust the update magnitude when it both aligns with the consensus direction and remains proportionate to the consensus signal. Experiments on math competition benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25) show that AVSD consistently outperforms both single-view self-distillation baselines and GRPO, achieving average Avg@8 gains of 3.1% and 2.2% over the strongest baselines on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, respectively. Moreover, on code-generation benchmarks (Codeforces, LiveCodeBench v6) using Qwen3-8B, AVSD outperforms the single-view self-distillation baseline by 2.4% on average.

item.title: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.00384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to propose statistical models, but these systems struggle on challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents), a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating reusable diagnostic tools. We evaluate VESTA using three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers that culminates in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines for statistical analysis and visual tool creation, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. Against strong agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode), VESTA is better on all time series tasks and on complex distribution fitting tasks, though the harnesses achieve better fits on simpler distributions. Further, dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VESTA VLM critic can reason over directly.

item.title: Balance of Benchmarks: Evidence Retention and Multiplicity-Aware Model Comparison [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.30044v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmark aggregation requires decisions about how much evidence to use and how much influence each benchmark receives. Curated suites control influence through selection, which can exclude informative observations. A broader pool can retain those observations. With equal weighting, repeated or closely related benchmarks gain influence as their number grows. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB) to retain eligible observations and control their influence separately. We fit benchmark-specific response curves to place different difficulty ranges on a shared ability scale and use description similarity to downweight benchmarks in crowded neighborhoods. We test retention and density weighting in separate interventions on WildScores, a sparse collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks, using 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks as a controlled reference. With the model population fixed and entire source-lineage families held out, suite expansion improves held-out prediction under BoB and equal-weight equating on both WildScores and BIG-bench. Under substantial reporting overlap, density weighting improves robustness to multiplicity. Complete re-listings yield smaller mean rank displacement under BoB (0.63 versus 1.95 for equal-weight equating), with benefits also in paraphrased re-listings and supported affine fits. The benefit can reverse if models report different benchmarks, because a single weight per column gives models that report only part of a group less than its intended share. We therefore compute each model's weights from the benchmarks it reports. This rule removes the reversal in controlled re-listings and keeps held-out prediction close to that of equal weighting. These comparisons separate evidence retention, benchmark influence, and reporting coverage and show why repeated entries need to be handled per model.

item.title: Clause-Factored Bilateral State Grounding and Scoped Passivity for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.37351v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-World Assumption (OWA) deduction requires distinguishing provable facts (True), refutations (False), and unprovable statements (Unknown) across counterfactual edits and unseen domains. Sequence and latent-recurrent transformers rely on distributional shortcuts, whereas chain-of-thought language models incur high autoregressive latency. We decompose OWA deduction into a clause-factored bilateral grounder ($F$) and a deductive deliberation operator ($B$), forming $B \circ F$ in Typed Edge-Factorized Bilateral Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD). Trained solely on three-way query labels without parsers or proof-depth annotations, TE-BPHD (37.85M parameters) maps clauses into a 1,440-dimensional Belnap space and propagates support through passivity-balanced implicit Port-Hamiltonian rule diodes. Across 17,036 locked ProofWriter test queries, TE-BPHD reaches 79.17 +/- 5.48% depth-5 counterfactual consistency (+23.83 to +38.67 percentage points over Seq2Seq T5, Flan-T5, and Recurrent-Depth T5) and 94.95 +/- 1.23% out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy across 5,270 six-domain queries (92.54 +/- 3.38% macro-mean). On a paired 120-query OOD slice, TE-BPHD attains 93.61 +/- 4.59% versus 79.17% for 3-shot Qwen3-1.7B under a 2,048-token reasoning cap (+14.44 percentage points) at 9.44 versus 14,878.4 ms/query batch-16 NVIDIA L4 throughput. Operator interventions show that symmetric single-rule passivity prevents positive two-cycle modes seen in Gain-Matched Unilateral Horn (+50.00 percentage points counterfactual consistency), whereas unit-interval Grounded Product-T-Norm Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) achieve cycle-safe OOD transfer (94.50 +/- 0.87%) without linear solves, and multi-fact ParaRules prose exposes an upstream grounding trade-off (1.33 +/- 1.76% zero-shot vs. 34.11 +/- 5.01% with five-slot optimal-transport joint grounding).

item.title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.39394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? Preliminary experiments show that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To trace this effect, we hold each problem fixed and vary its preceding history. The resulting changes in the model's internal states contain a recurring, problem-dependent component. To improve reasoning with retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). It captures attention keys and values from earlier response generation in a read-only bank. STAIR learns to reflect current query vectors to redirect attention over this bank during prompt processing. The backbone and stored entries remain fixed; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four reasoning benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history. The math-trained Qwen3.5-9B controller also improves code generation on HumanEval+ without further training.

item.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.32113v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. How does the safety effect of a single activation edit vary across early reasoning states, and what factors govern that variation? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, site-specific edits concentrate safety gains in the opening CoT tokens. Norm-matched controls on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (8B) disentangle two factors behind this curve: holding an effective direction and edit budget fixed still yields much larger early ($t_1$-$t_5$) than later ($t_6$-$t_8$) gains, whereas the near-zero site-specific $t_3$ gain reflects higher optimisation variance despite rising risk-probe AUROC. Forced prefixes shift the high-gain region with the opening context, and a four-arm intervention shows that ~98% of the net gain at $t_2$ propagates through the changed next token. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

item.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.18639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

item.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

item.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

item.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
item.description: arXiv:2611.23615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled projector rows and noise in the vision encoder, infers the unknown scale factors, and returns most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values and accuracy to near its original level. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry, a cue that a real failure need not leave. When we round those bits away, each model answers our test questions as before, but the agent, unaided, no longer repairs either model: on LFM2-VL accuracy recovers by about 4 points, against 17 from the unrounded weights. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling. On SmolVLM the agent uses it once a sentence in the prompt, which we wrote knowing the fault, names such a statistic; on LFM2-VL, whose scale factors are larger, most sessions find the rescaled rows unaided, but none finds the noise. Swapped rows or columns, which keep the set of stored values, are not found unaided on either model within our budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.

item.title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.23845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence. We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising. Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

item.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22432v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

item.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22897v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

item.title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.12805v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $\Phi$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

item.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.22639v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

item.title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git

item.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run. In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens. Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale. These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.

item.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

item.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

item.title: The ROI of Small Examples: Optimizing In-Context Learning Under Token Budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves large language model performance at inference time without updating model parameters. However, these gains are not free: in practical deployments, longer prompts directly increase inference cost and latency. Under a fixed token budget, prompt construction therefore becomes a resource-allocation problem. While prior work has often focused on how many examples to include in ICL, we study the complementary question of whether the available budget is better spent on a few long demonstrations or on a larger number of shorter ones. We study this aspect in question answering (QA), by organizing candidate demonstrations into length-based bins and constructing prompts from examples within the same length range under fixed budgets. Experiments on two QA benchmarks (\textit{Beat the AI} and \textit{Natural Questions}), using six instruction-tuned LLMs, show that shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space. This effect is especially strong on \textit{Beat the AI}, and remains visible on NQ, although gains are smaller and saturate earlier in the long-context setting. An additional natural language inference experiment on ANLI R3 finds that one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models, although longer demonstrations remain competitive. Overall, our results highlight demonstration granularity as an important factor in prompt design.

item.title: No-Harm-Jury A Jury-Based Multi-Dimensional Harm Evaluation Framework for Medical AI Responses [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present No-Harm-Jury, a jury-based automated evaluation framework that scores AI-generated medical responses across seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions using a panel of five diverse language models as independent jurors. Responses generated by Ministral-14B on 3,000 questions drawn from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA are scored by five jurors across dimensions of informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm; the 151 empty responses (98 MedQA, 53 MedM- CQA) are excluded, leaving 2,849 valid samples. The median aggregation robustly suppresses individual juror biases while maintaining coverage through complementary specialisation. No existing system combines all five prop- erties of No-Harm-Jury: automated scalable evaluation, five diverse LLM jurors, robust me- dian aggregation (with a reliability-weighted extension), seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions, and application to medical QA benchmarks.

item.title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

item.title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.24994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

item.title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

item.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

item.title: Incorporating argumentation frameworks for LLM decision-making: Task-specific design and evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.

item.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

item.title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

item.title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.25557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.

item.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
